claims.text: Enhanced oxidation resistance in HEAs is caused by synergistic segregation of multiple oxide-forming reactive elements such as Cr, Al, and Ti.
The segregating reactive elements collectively form and maintain a continuous, dense, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
The HEA initially has a near-homogeneous distribution of multiple oxide-forming reactive elements.
High configurational entropy maintains elemental homogeneity in the HEA at lower temperatures.
At high temperatures, the homogeneity-promoting effect of configurational entropy is overcome by selective oxidation kinetics.
Selective oxidation causes the reactive elements to preferentially segregate to the alloy surface.
The surface-enriched reactive elements evolve into a mixed oxide layer whose constituent oxides interact synergistically.
Complementary effects among the constituent oxides make the oxide layer dense and adherent.
The dense, adherent oxide layer limits further oxygen ingress and thereby protects the underlying alloy.
Relative to a conventional lower-entropy alloy with similar oxide-forming constituents, the HEA will form a more uniform and stable oxide layer.
The HEA oxide layer will grow more slowly than the oxide layer on the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA oxide layer will adhere better than the oxide layer on the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA will exhibit less oxidation-associated weight gain than the conventional-alloy baseline.
A traditional low-entropy alloy with similar oxide-forming elements is expected to form a more porous, discontinuous, or otherwise less effective oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-temperature oxidizing conditions, exemplified by temperatures of at least 800°C.
The proposed effect may be weaker at lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments.
An optimal concentration of reactive elements is required for synergistic protective-film formation.
Testing the HEA and a lower-complexity conventional alloy under identical controlled oxidizing conditions provides the proposed controlled comparison.
Oxide thickness, uniformity, composition, elemental segregation, adhesion, and weight-gain kinetics are measurable indicators of the proposed mechanism.
Failure of the HEA to produce a significantly more continuous, adherent, and slow-growing scale than the conventional alloy would falsify the proposed segregation-based explanation.
